extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate or graduate students and researchers in enumerative combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt on sieve methods (Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion, rook polynomials, Ferrers boards, V-partitions, and related combinatorial techniques) giving theorems, examples, and constructive bijections used to count combinatorial objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion (linear-transform formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The linear transformation φ on the 2^n-dimensional space of functions f:2^S → K defined by φf(T)=∑_{Y⊇T} f(Y) has inverse φ^{-1} given by φ^{-1}f(T)=∑_{Y⊇T} (−1)^{|Y−T|} f(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: think of S as a set of properties and f^{=}(T) as the weighted number of objects having exactly the properties in T, f^{≥}(T) as those having at least the properties in T. Then the inverse formula yields explicit inclusion–exclusion sums (equations (2.3)–(2.5)) such as the number of objects having none of the properties: f^{=}(∅)=∑_{Y⊆S} (−1)^{|Y|} f^{≥}(Y). Theorem 2.1.1 is the algebraic core; typical combinatorial use is to start with an overcount and subtract successive overcounts until convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual form of Inclusion–Exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: If φf(T)=∑_{Y⊆T} f(Y) for all T⊆S, then φ^{-1}f(T)=∑_{Y⊆T} (−1)^{|T−Y|} f(Y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dualizes the preceding formulation by interchanging ⊇ and ⊆. Use this when counting objects with properties 'at most' a given set rather than 'at least.' Yields formulas (2.8) and expressions for f^{≤} and f^{=}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special symmetric case / finite-differences equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When f^{=}(T) (or f^{≥}(T)) depends only on |T|, set a(i) or b(i) accordingly; then the inclusion–exclusion sums reduce to binomial transforms (equations (2.9)–(2.10)). The inverse matrix entries are (−1)^{i−j} C(i,j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to the equivalence a(m)=∑_{i=0}^m (−1)^{m−i} C(m,i) b(i) and the interpretation a(m)=Δ^m b(0) in the calculus of finite differences. Useful whenever symmetry implies counts depend only on the number of specified properties, not on which ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derangement formula and approximations (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number D(n) of permutations with no fixed points (derangements) equals D(n)=n! ∑_{i=0}^n (−1)^i / i! (equation (2.12)); recurrence D(n)=(n−1)(D(n−1)+D(n−2)) and asymptotically D(n)≈n!/e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model fixed point conditions as properties and apply the symmetric-case inclusion–exclusion. Generating-function form is ∑ D(n) x^n/n! = e^{−1}/(1−x)?? (explicit series given). Use this classical example as a template for property-counting problems where b(i)=i!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: Δ^n rule (Proposition 2.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a family B_n the numbers of elements lacking at most the properties in any T depend only on |T| (so b(i) independent of n in the appropriate sense), then the number a(n) of elements having none of the properties satisfies a(n)=Δ^n b(0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a compact finite-difference computation method when b(i) depends only on i; see applications to permutations and other symmetric settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: when b(i) depends on n (Example 2.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the counts b(i) depend on ambient parameters (e.g., n) then Proposition 2.2.2 does not apply; resulting inclusion–exclusion expressions still hold but Δ^n applied to a sequence depending on n is more complicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: permutations of a multiset (no two consecutive equal) where b(i) = g(n,i) depends on n; inclusion–exclusion still yields an explicit sum but not the simple Δ^n b(0) form. Be careful to check parameter independence assumptions before applying Δ^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant formula for permutations with a given descent set (Example 2.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S={s1<...<sk}⊆[n−1], the number β_n(S) of permutations with descent set exactly S equals β_n(S)=n! · det[1/(s_{j+1}−s_i)!]_{0≤i,j≤k} (equation (2.16)), with s_0=0, s_{k+1}=n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by Möbius inversion on subsets and the product decomposition α_n(S)=Π (differences factorial) for permutations whose descent set is contained in S. The determinant representation can be reworked via a generic function f with f(i,i)=1 to obtain alternate forms (2.15)–(2.17). Useful when converting inclusion–exclusion sums into determinants.

rubrics_metrics.name: q-analogue via inversion statistic (Example 2.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define β_n(S,q)=∑_{w : D(w)=S} q^{inv(w)}. Then with the same indices s_i one obtains a q-analogue determinant: β_n(S,q) = [n]!_q · det[1/([s_{j+1}−s_i]!) ] (equation (2.21) – matrix entries written in q-factorial form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the inversion statistic and standardization/ shuffle arguments to lift determinant formulas to q-analogues. Provides generating polynomials with combinatorial coefficients (explicit example n=8,S={1,5}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-to-determinant criterion (Proposition 2.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for a property family indexed increasing s_i one has f^{=}(T)=h(n)·∏ e(s_i,s_{i+1}) for T={s1,...,sk}, with e(i,i)=1 and e(i,j)=0 for j<i, then f^{=}(T) can be written as h(n)·det[e(si,s_{j+1})]_{0≤i,j≤k}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why determinants appear in earlier examples: when the 'contained-in' counts factor multiplicatively across consecutive blocks, the inclusion–exclusion inversion becomes a determinant. Use to recognize when determinant formulas apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rook polynomial identity (Theorem 2.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a board B⊆[n]×[n] with rook numbers r_k (number of ways to place k nonattacking rooks on B) and counts N_j (permutations whose graph has exactly j squares in B), the polynomial identity holds: N_n(x)=∑_{k=0}^n r_k (n−k)! (x−1)^k (equation (2.22)). In particular N_0 = ∑_{k=0}^n (−1)^k r_k (n−k)! (equation (2.23)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two combinatorial proofs: counting extensions of chosen k-rook placements or labeling arguments; plug x=1 or x=0 to get specialized enumerations. This is the standard bridge between rook theory and inclusion–exclusion counting of permutations with forbidden positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derangements via rook numbers (Example 2.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the board of forbidden fixed-points B={(1,1),...,(n,n)}, we have r_k = C(n,k) implying N_0 = D(n)=∑_{k=0}^n (−1)^k n!/k!, recovering the classical derangement formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialize Theorem 2.3.1 to standard diagonal board to obtain the derangement sum; illustrates the rook-polynomial approach to classical inclusion–exclusion problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menage problem setup and circular nonconsecutive selection lemma (Lemma 2.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For m points on a circle, the number of ways to choose k points with no two consecutive equals (explicit closed form given in Lemma 2.3.4) (combinatorial proofs provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs: a counting with an auxiliary blue point and a circular→linear reduction. Use this when counting k-subsets with spacing constraints on a circle (applies to menage/ k-discordant permutation boards). The lemma is used to compute rook numbers for boards with cyclic adjacency constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-discordant permutations and rook polynomial encoding (Corollary discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For board B_{n,k} forbidding positions (i,i),(i,i+1),...,(i,i+k−1) (mod n), the rook polynomial R_{n,k}(x)=∑ r_i(n,k) x^i encodes the number f(n,k) of permutations with w(i) ≡ i (mod constraints) via f(n,k)=∑_{i≥0} (−1)^i r_i(n,k)(n−i)! (equation linking rook numbers to permutations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines k-discordant permutations; when k>2 closed forms for r_i are not simple but there exist generating polynomials Q_k(x,y) giving R_{n,k}(x) realizations (reference to later Example 4.7.19). Use rook polynomial machinery to study seating/adjacency-restricted permutation problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ferrers board rook-factorization (Theorem 2.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Ferrers board B of shape (b_1,...,b_m) set s_i=b_i−(i−1); the rook polynomial ∑ r_k x^k satisfies ∑ r_k x^k = ∑_{k} r_k · (x)_m−k = ∏_{i=1}^m (x + s_i) (equation in Theorem 2.4.1, expressed equivalently as coefficient-wise identity using falling factorials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses adding an x×m rectangle beneath the shape and counting placements by columns. This gives a product form for generating polynomial factors and is a fundamental structural result for Ferrers boards; practical consequences include closed-form rook numbers and combinatorial interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stirling numbers relation for staircase Ferrers board (Corollary 2.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the triangular/staircase board of shape (0,1,2,...,m−1) the rook numbers are rk = S(m,m−k) (Stirling numbers of second kind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Theorem 2.4.1 since each s_i=0 and ∑ r_k (x)_{m−k} = x^m. Useful bijective intuition: placements of k rooks correspond to partitions into m−k blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness criteria for Ferrers boards via s_i-multisets (Corollary 2.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Ferrers boards (with m columns) have the same rook polynomial iff their multisets {s_i} are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of the factorization in Theorem 2.4.1. Leads to enumeration questions about how many Ferrers shapes share a given rook polynomial (addressed in Theorem 2.4.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Count of Ferrers boards with same rook polynomial (Theorem 2.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a Ferrers shape (c_1,...,c_m) augmented with leading zeros to (b_1,...,b_t) and grouping equal s_j values, the number f(c_1,...,c_m) of Ferrers boards with no empty columns having the same rook polynomial equals a product-of-binomial-quotients formula (explicit product of binomial coefficients and reciprocals shown in theorem statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch proof uses placing multiplicities a_i of equal s-values and counting permissible orderings subject to column-length constraints. Useful for enumerating all Ferrers boards with identical rook polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical increasing Ferrers representative (Corollary 2.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Ferrers board has a unique Ferrers board with distinct nonzero column lengths (strictly increasing then nonincreasing pattern) sharing the same rook polynomial; e.g., the board [n] corresponds to shape (1,3,5,...,2n−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from arranging the multiset of s_i so columns strictly increase to maximum then nonincrease; gives a canonical representative among equivalent rook-polynomial classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: V-partitions and unimodal sequences generating-function sieve (Propositions 2.5.1–2.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define V-partitions as unimodal sequences rooted at a largest part; v(n) counts V-partitions and V(q)=∑ v(n) q^n has product/sieve representation V(q)=∑_{k≥0} q^{k}/([k]!^2) and equivalently V(q)=∏_{i≥1} (1−q^{i})^{−2} multiplied by alternating q^{(n+1 choose 2)} terms (explicit sieve-derived product formula in Proposition 2.5.1). The total number U(q) of unimodal sequences satisfies U(q)+V(q)=∏_{i≥1} (1−q^i)^{−2} and hence U(q) is given by an alternating sum/product formula (Corollary 2.5.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counting uses a sieve by double partitions D_n and surjective maps Γ_i with controlled multiplicities, producing alternating inclusion–exclusion-like sums; this is an example of a sieve process that is not a straightforward PIE application. Use the constructions/ bijections in the section to convert between double partitions, V-partitions, and unimodal sequences and derive generating functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution/bijection proof of inclusion–exclusion identity (Section 2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A direct combinatorial bijection (involution) σ between signed combinatorial constructions gives a bijective proof of the inclusion–exclusion identity ∑_{|Y| odd} f^{≥}(Y)=∑_{|Y| even} f^{≥}(Y) once terms are rearranged so signs are positive (equation (2.30)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct σ on ordered triples (x,Y,Z) with cases depending on minima of Y and Z; σ is its own inverse up to the defined cases. This section demonstrates the standard involution principle technique to turn algebraic PIE identities into explicit bijections, useful for combinatorial proofs and algorithmic cancellations.
